meta.theme: food prohibitions versus food procedures as boundary markers: the first is kept alone and portable, the second requires co-performers, so dispersal dissolves a shared practice into a stated identity without anyone abandoning anything

meta.reviewer_notes: A contrast passage whose two terms are easy to state and hard to keep apart under pressure. The set turns on cost: abstention is paid by one person, coordination by a group, and almost every distractor is built by forgetting which is which.

quality.adversarial_review: Three readings of the passage now compete in every question. The shadow reading is the elegy: dispersal empties a shared life, what survives is a shell kept up out of habit, so a tradition that still looks intact has already died and the prohibitions must follow. It holds an option in each question (Q1 'empties a shared life', Q2 'elegiac', Q3 'has already stopped organising anyone's day', Q4 the belief condition, Q5 'outlast the shared life') and it dies on two sentences in the last paragraph: 'What has happened is not a loss of belief but a change in what the rules are for', and 'Nothing is renounced, nobody is persuaded of anything'. The second rival makes the outsider's gaze the cause — what survives is what outsiders can see and ask about — and it reverses the passage's own order: prohibitions are 'the part of a tradition most visible from outside' because they are portable, not portable because they are visible, and the third paragraph explains a procedure's failure by shifts and distances with no outsider in it. The third rival takes the opening concession for the thesis and keeps the classificatory account whole; the second sentence limits it by name, saying it 'has been asked to go further than it can'. Q2's live rival remains the elegiac option, since the closing cadence has the rhythm of a lament, and it is settled by what the author calls the event: a change, an assimilation needing no convert, a wall that comes down 'by the ordinary operation of timetables'. Q5's key is now a definition of the word rather than a restatement of the argument, and the three distractors carry the argument instead, so that a reader looking for the thesis in the vocabulary item is led away from the answer rather than towards it. Strength parity was imposed across the set afterwards: no distractor in this file is quantified more strongly than its key, because a single overreaching option was found to condemn the whole reading it belonged to without the passage being read.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement, but the reader reported that the tone question could be answered from the shape of its options alone: two loud caricatures and a hedge around one measured answer. All four options of that question have since been rewritten so that each distractor is a defensible misreading — the subject's sadness taken for the author's, a limit on an admired idea taken for impatience, careful prose taken for hesitation — and the item awaits a re-solve. Options rebuilt against an explicit shadow thesis (a coherent rival reading carried across every question in the passage) so that the option sets no longer form a single consistent clique; the item awaits a re-solve. A second pass then removed the strength asymmetry two blind readers named as the residual channel: every distractor is now hedged no more strongly than its key, and where the passage itself asserts something flatly the key carries the absolute, so that the most cautious option is no longer reliably the answer. A third pass closed four key-to-key paraphrase and entailment leaks between questions, replaced the true options of the NOT item with framing rather than mechanism, and removed two distractors that hardening had made true. A fourth pass repaired two distractors that hardening had made defensible (an inference option entailed on a causal reading, and a purpose option with no false half) and removed a shape cue from the NOT item.

passage.title: What Travels and What Does Not

paragraphs.text: The most durable anthropological insight about food is that rules of eating are rules of classification: a community decides what belongs where, and its table keeps the register. The insight is sound as far as it goes, and it has been asked to go further than it can, because it treats as one thing two rules that behave quite differently under strain. Some food rules are prohibitions, and say what may not be eaten. Others are procedures, and say how what is eaten must be got, handled, cooked, served and shared — in which vessel, by whose hands, in what order, in whose company. Both mark the edge of a group. They do not mark it in the same way.

A prohibition is portable. It asks nothing of the keeper's surroundings and nothing of anybody else: it can be observed in a canteen, in a foreign city, at a table where no one knows what is being done and no one would mind if they did. Its cost is abstention, and abstention is a cost one person can pay alone. This is why prohibitions are the part of a tradition most visible from outside and the part most easily described; they can be stated as a list, and a list can be carried anywhere. It is also why they are so often mistaken for the whole of the matter, and why an outsider, seeing a refusal and no ceremony, concludes that the rule is about squeamishness.

A procedure cannot be kept alone. It needs other people who know what they are doing: someone to prepare the food as the rule specifies, others to receive it in the order the rule specifies, a household with the vessels and the hours and the memory the rule presumes. Its cost is not abstention but coordination, and coordination is paid by a group. A procedure therefore fails for reasons that have nothing to do with conviction. Nobody need decide that it no longer matters; it is enough that the people whose participation it requires are working different shifts, or living an hour away, or not there at all.

The consequence is an asymmetry that is hard to see from inside. Put a community under dispersal and the procedures go first while the prohibitions remain; and because the prohibitions remain, and because they are what outsiders ask about, the tradition can look intact from either side of the boundary long after it has stopped organising anyone's day. What has happened is not a loss of belief but a change in what the rules are for. A boundary once maintained by what people did together has become a boundary carried by individuals, one at a time, in the form of something they can state about themselves. Assimilation of this kind needs no convert and no crisis. Nothing is renounced, nobody is persuaded of anything, and the wall comes down from the inside by the ordinary operation of timetables.

questions.target_mistake: offering the passage's most striking consequence as its purpose, adopting the classificatory account the author grants in the opening sentence, or crediting the outsider's attention with the survival that the passage explains by cost
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: the author is prising apart two kinds of rule that are usually treated as one, in order to explain something the undivided account cannot explain.
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is

options.A: to describe how dispersal empties a shared life of its practices, and to show why what survives makes the loss hard to see
options.B: to defend the view that rules of eating express a system of classification, and to explain why outsiders take such rules for squeamishness
options.C: to show that a tradition under strain keeps the part of itself outsiders can see, and loses the part hidden from them
options.D: to separate two kinds of food rule usually treated as one, and to show what the distinction explains about the way a boundary fails

explanation.expert_notice: The opening paragraph announces the project in a single complaint: the classificatory insight 'has been asked to go further than it can, because it treats as one thing two rules that behave quite differently under strain'. Everything that follows is that separation being carried out and then cashed in.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names the operation and its pay-off. Two paragraphs define the two kinds of rule by their cost — abstention for one, coordination for the other — and the last paragraph uses the distinction to explain a specific failure, in which a boundary survives as a statement about oneself after it has stopped organising anyone's day. Every option here offers two jobs joined by 'and', so the pairing is no guide; what settles it is whether the pair spans the passage and gets its direction right. One names a consequence twice over and calls it a loss the passage declines to call one; one reverses the passage's order of cause and visibility; and one keeps whole the account the second sentence limits by name.
explanation.question_type_note: Primary-purpose questions want the verb and its object across the whole passage. In a contrast passage the verb is almost always distinguishing, and the object is the pair the author says has been run together.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage opens by saying an accepted idea has been asked to do too much, expect the purpose to be a division rather than a discovery. Then check any candidate purpose against the paragraph map: if you can point to the one paragraph it came from, it is a job the passage does, not the job the passage is for.

distractors.why_wrong: Both halves belong to the final paragraph, where the consequence is drawn, and the first half misdescribes it: the passage refuses the word loss for what happens, calling it 'a change in what the rules are for' in which 'nothing is renounced'. The distinction between prohibition and procedure is built over two paragraphs before dispersal is mentioned at all, and the opening paragraph announces that distinction as the thing to be made.
distractors.seductive_element: These are the passage's most concrete and most memorable claims, and a pair of striking claims joined by 'and' reads like a summary of the whole.

distractors.why_wrong: The classificatory account is granted in the opening sentence and limited in the next one; the author neither defends it nor attacks it, but argues that it cannot tell two kinds of rule apart. The squeamishness remark is real, and it is an aside in a paragraph whose work is defining what portability costs.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does open with that account and does call it sound, and the squeamishness sentence sounds like the author taking the community's side against a hostile reading.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage runs this the other way. Prohibitions are 'the part of a tradition most visible from outside and the part most easily described' because they are portable, and a procedure fails because 'the people whose participation it requires are working different shifts, or living an hour away, or not there at all'. No outsider appears in the explanation of what lapses.
distractors.seductive_element: The second paragraph really does dwell on what outsiders see, and the last paragraph says the tradition 'can look intact from either side of the boundary', so the outside gaze is present throughout without ever being the cause.

questions.target_mistake: taking the subject's sadness for the author's, hearing amusement at the outsider's error where the passage explains it, or taking a limit placed on an admired idea for agreement with it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before the options: the author describes a loss without grieving it, corrects an accepted idea without heat, and rests his whole argument on the distinction he draws.
questions.stem: The author's tone in the passage is best described as

options.A: elegiac, mourning a shared life that ends without anyone deciding to end it
options.B: wry about a tradition that survives chiefly in the form outsiders ask to see
options.C: matter-of-fact and unsentimental, explaining the change rather than grieving over it
options.D: expository, carrying an established insight further rather than marking out a limit to it

explanation.expert_notice: Look for the evaluative words and count how few there are. The classificatory insight is 'the most durable' one in its field and 'sound as far as it goes' before any limit is placed on it. The outsider's error about squeamishness is explained rather than judged. And a whole cultural dissolution is accounted for by 'the ordinary operation of timetables', which is the flattest available way of saying it.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names the method and the temperature in one phrase. The analysis is plain: one category is divided into two, each half is defined by what it costs, and a consequence is derived from the difference. What the final paragraph then does is the deciding evidence. It reaches the place where a reader expects feeling and supplies mechanism instead, calling the event 'a change in what the rules are for' and explaining it by shifts and distances; the word loss is never used of it. Explaining rather than grieving is exactly the conduct of those four sentences.
explanation.question_type_note: Tone is set by judgement words, not by topic. A passage can describe something sad in a voice that is not sad, and the options will always offer you the emotion the subject matter suggests.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what the author calls the thing, not what the thing is, and check the compliments as well as the complaints. If the strongest evaluative phrase about a loss is 'ordinary', the grieving option is gone; if the criticised idea is also called the most durable in its field, so is the angry one.

distractors.why_wrong: Mourning is the reading the last paragraph invites and then declines. Nothing there is called a loss: what happens is 'a change in what the rules are for', an assimilation that 'needs no convert and no crisis', a wall that comes down 'by the ordinary operation of timetables'. Those are mechanisms. An author who wanted the reader to grieve had four sentences in which to say so and spent every one of them explaining.
distractors.seductive_element: The closing cadence, with nothing renounced and nobody persuaded, has the rhythm of an elegy, and the event it describes is one a reader arrives ready to be sad about.

distractors.why_wrong: There is no amusement anywhere in the passage's account of outsiders. The one place an outsider appears in error, concluding from a refusal and no ceremony that the rule is about squeamishness, the mistake is explained by what is visible rather than mocked; and the survival of the prohibitions is attributed to their cost being payable alone, not to anyone's asking about them.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does keep returning to what a tradition looks like from outside, and an author who notices being looked at is often amused by it.

distractors.why_wrong: The compliment is real and the extension is invented. The insight is called the most durable in its field and 'sound as far as it goes', and the very next clause says it 'has been asked to go further than it can'. A limit placed in the second sentence of a passage is not an extension, and the four paragraphs that follow are spent showing what the undivided account cannot distinguish.
distractors.seductive_element: The opening sentence is generous and the passage never calls the classificatory account false, so a reader who registers the compliment without the qualification that carries it hears a field's own idea being taken further.

questions.target_mistake: making visibility to outsiders the thing that decides what survives, turning the fourth paragraph's remark about appearances into a test for hollowness, or generalising the outsider's error into a rule about what outsiders see
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that a supported inference follows from who pays the cost: a rule one person can keep says something about that person, and a rule requiring several says something about whether they are still together.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A rule survives dispersal in proportion to how visible it is to people outside the community.
options.B: A rule that can be kept alone shows less about what a community still does together than one that cannot.
options.C: What a food rule marks about a community does not depend on which kind of rule it is.
options.D: A tradition that still looks intact to outsiders has already stopped organising anyone's day.

explanation.expert_notice: The passage defines each kind of rule by who pays for it. A prohibition costs abstention, 'a cost one person can pay alone'; a procedure costs coordination, and 'coordination is paid by a group'. The last paragraph turns that into a warning about what a surviving rule proves: the tradition 'can look intact from either side of the boundary long after it has stopped organising anyone's day'.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option follows from the two costs. A prohibition still kept tells you only that one person went without something, which one person can do in a canteen among strangers; a procedure still performed tells you that the people it needs were there, with the vessels and the hours and the memory it presumes, because there is no other way it could have happened. So the rule anyone can keep alone reports least about what the passage calls a boundary maintained by what people did together, which is exactly why a tradition reduced to its prohibitions can look intact after it has stopped organising anyone's day.
explanation.question_type_note: Inference questions on a contrast passage are decided by the axis of the contrast; here the axis is cost, and every option has to be tested against who pays.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author distinguishes two things by a single property, write that property down and check each option against it. Options that swap the two sides of the axis feel right because both halves are in the passage.

distractors.why_wrong: Survival is explained by cost, not by visibility: a prohibition lasts because abstention 'is a cost one person can pay alone', and a procedure fails because the people it needs are on different shifts or an hour away. Visibility is a consequence of portability in the passage's own order, not its cause.
distractors.seductive_element: The two properties travel together throughout — the rules that survive are also the rules outsiders ask about — and a correlation stated twice is easily promoted to an explanation.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the undivided account the passage exists to divide. The first paragraph grants that both kinds of rule 'mark the edge of a group' and then adds the sentence the whole argument rests on: 'They do not mark it in the same way.' A prohibition still kept marks what one person will go without; a procedure still performed marks that the people it needs were there.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the received insight the opening sentence calls the most durable in its field, and an idea the author compliments before limiting is easily carried away without the limit.

distractors.why_wrong: This runs the fourth paragraph's sentence backwards. The passage says that a community put under dispersal can look intact long after its procedures have gone; it never says that looking intact is a symptom of that, and a community whose procedures are all still running looks intact to outsiders for the straightforward reason that it is.
distractors.seductive_element: It is built entirely from the passage's most memorable sentence, and an appearance the author warns about is easily promoted into a test the author never offers.

questions.target_mistake: importing belief as the cause of a lapse the passage attributes to logistics, making outside attention the condition of survival, or narrowing the boundary work to what may be eaten
questions.stem: If the passage is true, which of the following must also be true?

options.A: A procedure lapses only when a community has stopped believing in what the procedure expresses.
options.B: A food rule that outsiders take no interest in is one a dispersed community drops.
options.C: A community whose food rules are all prohibitions could maintain them without its members ever assembling.
options.D: A community's food rules mark its boundary only in so far as they classify what may be eaten.

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph is a set of necessary conditions in disguise: a prohibition 'asks nothing of the keeper's surroundings and nothing of anybody else', and its cost 'is a cost one person can pay alone'. Anything that follows from those two clauses alone must be true if the passage is.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that entailment. If every rule a community holds is of a kind that requires no other participant and no particular setting, then nothing in the observance of those rules requires the members to come together at all. The passage says as much when it describes a prohibition being kept in a canteen or a foreign city among people who do not know what is being done.
explanation.question_type_note: A must-be-true question is a test, not a preference: ask whether the passage could be entirely true while the option is false. If it could, the option is not forced, however likely it sounds.
explanation.reading_habit: Run each option through the negation test rather than the plausibility test. Words like 'only when', 'will not keep' and 'only in so far as' are where an option quietly asks for more than the text guarantees.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph rules this out in terms: a procedure 'fails for reasons that have nothing to do with conviction', and the reasons given are shifts, distance and absence rather than any change of mind. The last paragraph repeats it — what has happened 'is not a loss of belief'.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because belief is the explanation most readers bring to questions about tradition, and the passage does discuss what the rules express.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the passage makes outside attention bear on what a community keeps. What survives dispersal is what one person can pay for alone, and the passage's canteen and foreign city are places where a prohibition is kept precisely among people who do not know it is being kept and would not mind if they did — outside interest at its lowest, and the rule kept anyway.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage twice notes that prohibitions are what outsiders ask about, so a reader may take the thing correlated with survival for the thing that produces it.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage gives both kinds of rule the same boundary-marking work — 'Both mark the edge of a group. They do not mark it in the same way' — and a procedure governs how food is got, handled, cooked, served and shared rather than what may be eaten. Restricting the boundary to what may be eaten deletes half the passage's subject.
distractors.seductive_element: It states the received classificatory account the opening sentence calls sound, and an account the author grants is easily taken for one the author is committed to.

questions.target_mistake: answering the vocabulary question with the passage's argument instead of with the word's meaning in its sentence, or taking a consequence of portability for the thing the word names
questions.prediction_target: The learner should paraphrase the word from the sentence after it, which spells out what portability consists of: no demand on the surroundings and none on other people.
questions.stem: In the second paragraph, "portable" most nearly means

options.A: able to outlast the shared life that once gave the rule its point
options.B: easily stated to outsiders, and so easily carried from one place to another
options.C: expressing a classification that holds good wherever in the world the keeper happens to be
options.D: unaffected by where it is kept, since it makes no demand on its setting

explanation.expert_notice: The word is defined by the sentence that follows it, which names two demands a prohibition does not make: 'It asks nothing of the keeper's surroundings and nothing of anybody else.' The word portable answers to the first of those.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the first half of that definition put back into the word. Portability here is indifference to place: because the rule requires no particular setting, it can be observed in a canteen, in a foreign city, at a table where nobody knows what is being done. What a prohibition asks of other people is a separate clause and a separate matter, and the passage keeps the two apart because a procedure fails on the second while remaining innocent of the first.
explanation.question_type_note: A word-in-context question is decided by the sentence that surrounds the word. Where a passage has a thesis, the standard decoy is the thesis in the word's clothes: an option that would be a good summary of the argument is usually a bad definition of the term.
explanation.reading_habit: When a familiar word appears in an argument, read the next sentence before you translate it, and take only the part of that sentence the word is doing. Authors who use a plain word narrowly explain the narrowing immediately, and the explanation is usually smaller than the argument it goes on to support.

distractors.why_wrong: Portability is a property the rule has from the outset, and the sentence after the word says what it consists of: the rule 'asks nothing of the keeper's surroundings and nothing of anybody else'. Outlasting a shared life is something a portable rule turns out to do, four paragraphs later, and it is not what the word is being used to mean.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the passage's own story compressed into a definition, and a reader who has grasped the argument will recognise it before reading the sentence the word sits in.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph puts these the other way round: because a prohibition asks nothing of its setting, it is 'the part of a tradition most visible from outside and the part most easily described'. Being easy to state is a consequence the passage derives from portability, so it cannot be what portability means.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the near-tie, and it borrows the paragraph's own image of a list that can be carried anywhere, which sits two sentences from the word.

distractors.why_wrong: The word is applied to what a rule demands, not to what it asserts. A procedure expresses a classification too, and travels no better for it; what the passage says of the prohibition is that one person can keep it wherever they are, which is a fact about cost and setting rather than about the reach of a classification.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does open on the claim that rules of eating are rules of classification, so an option in that vocabulary sounds like the author's own account of the word.

vocabulary.passage_use: A prohibition is portable. It asks nothing of the keeper's surroundings
vocabulary.meaning_here: keepable anywhere, because it makes no demand on setting or on other people

vocabulary.passage_use: Its cost is abstention, and abstention is a cost one person can pay alone
vocabulary.meaning_here: the act of refraining from something; here, the whole price of keeping a prohibition

vocabulary.passage_use: Put a community under dispersal and the procedures go first
vocabulary.meaning_here: the scattering of a group's members so that they are no longer at hand

mentor.challenge: Two kinds of food rule are defined early and then kept apart for the rest of the passage. Decide which cost belongs to which rule, because nearly every question is decided by that one property.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Food prohibitions and food procedures both mark the edge of a group, but a prohibition costs only abstention and can be kept alone anywhere, while a procedure costs coordination and needs other people, so dispersal removes the procedures and leaves the prohibitions, turning a boundary that people maintained together into one that individuals merely state.
mentor.main_idea: Rules about what may not be eaten are kept by one person and travel anywhere. Rules about how food must be handled and shared need other people and cannot travel. When a community scatters, the second kind disappears and the first kind stays, so the tradition looks unbroken while the shared life behind it has stopped. Nobody has abandoned anything; the boundary has simply changed from a practice into a label.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Communities have rules about food. The writer says there are two very different kinds, and people usually talk about them as if they were one.

The first kind is a ban: this may not be eaten. You can keep a ban by yourself. You can keep it in a work canteen, in a strange city, sitting with people who have no idea what you are doing. It costs you one thing only, which is going without, and one person can pay that.

The second kind is a method: how the food must be bought, prepared, served and shared, in which dish, by whose hands, in what order, with whom. You cannot keep a method by yourself. You need other people who know the steps, and a house with the right things in it, and a time when everyone is there. Its cost is not going without; its cost is getting people together, and a group has to pay that.

So what happens when a community spreads out? The methods go first. Not because anybody stops believing in them — nobody has to decide anything — but because the people needed for them are on other shifts, or an hour away, or gone. The bans survive, because a ban needs nobody.

And here is the quiet part. Outsiders ask about bans, and the bans are still there, so from outside and even from inside the tradition looks whole. But it is no longer running anybody's day. What used to be a thing people did together has become a thing individuals can say about themselves. No one converted, no one argued, and the wall came down anyway, simply because of timetables.
mentor.why_difficult: The distinction is easy to understand and hard to hold. Both halves are in front of the reader at once, and under time pressure the properties swap: the paragraph on prohibitions dwells on how exposed and misunderstood they are, which makes them feel fragile, exactly when the argument needs them to be the durable half. The last paragraph then makes a second demanding move, separating a change in belief from a change in circumstance, and readers who assume traditions die of doubt will misread it. The tone compounds the difficulty, because the subject is a loss and the prose refuses to treat it as one.
mentor.author_intention: To stop the reader from treating a list of prohibitions as a measure of how intact a tradition is, and to show what an undivided account of food rules cannot explain.

paragraph_journey.note: Accepts the standard idea that food rules are rules of classification, then says it hides a difference: some rules ban a food, others prescribe how food is handled and shared.
A ban can be kept anywhere by one person, because it needs nothing and nobody. That is why outsiders see bans first and think the whole thing is about disgust.
A method needs other people, equipment and shared time. It can stop working without anyone changing their mind, simply because the participants are not available.
Scatter a community and the methods go while the bans stay, so the tradition looks intact from both sides. The boundary becomes something individuals state rather than something people do.

mentor.tone_progression: Even throughout: a mild correction of an accepted idea at the start, careful definition in the middle, and at the end the flattest possible account of a large loss, explained by shifts and distances rather than by any failure of faith.
key_transitions: 'The insight is sound as far as it goes, and it has been asked to go further than it can' (paragraph 1) — the concession that sets up the division.
'A procedure therefore fails for reasons that have nothing to do with conviction.' (paragraph 3) — belief is removed from the mechanism.
'The consequence is an asymmetry that is hard to see from inside.' (opening of paragraph 4) — the distinction is cashed in.
mentor.misunderstanding: The commonest wrong picture is that this is a passage about a tradition weakening because people believe in it less, with the food rules as evidence of the decline. The passage says the opposite about the cause: nothing is renounced and nobody is persuaded of anything. The second wrong picture reverses the asymmetry, because the paragraph on prohibitions emphasises how misunderstood and visible they are and a reader converts visibility into vulnerability. Both misreadings survive a first pass because every element of them really does appear somewhere in the text.
mentor.traps_summary: The set is built from three moves. Swapping the two sides of a contrast, since both are in the passage and only the axis tells them apart. Supplying a cause the author has explicitly excluded, here belief. And widening a claim from food procedures to all collective practice, or from 'outlasts procedures' to 'survives anything'. Before choosing, check which half of the contrast the option is about and what it has added to the text's own strength.
mentor.reading_lesson: In a passage built on a contrast, find the single property the author uses to separate the two terms and write it in the margin: here it is who pays the cost. Every later question, on inference, on entailment, even on a word's meaning, is decided by that property rather than by which term sounds more important. When an option feels right but you cannot say which side of the axis it sits on, it is usually the trap.
mentor.real_world: The same asymmetry governs languages, festivals and family customs anywhere people move for work: the parts that one person can keep alone survive the move, the parts that need a room full of people do not, and the survivors are mistaken for the whole.
mentor.takeaway: A rule you can keep alone tells you about a person; a rule you cannot tells you whether the group is still there.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the practices you inherited could you keep entirely by yourself, and which would end the moment nobody turned up?
